newsitem.title: SYRIA: Arabs, Israelis meet in Mideast diplomacy revival.
newsitem.headline: Arabs, Israelis meet in Mideast diplomacy revival.

text.p: Arabs and Israelis held a series of meetings on Tuesday in a revival of Middle East peace diplomacy after Israel suspended building a new Jewish enclave in Arab East Jerusalem.

Officials said a previously unannounced meeting in Damascus between Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Syria's Hafez al-Assad would focus on the deadlocked Syrian-Israeli peace talks and Israeli settlements in Arab areas.

The meeting followed a decision on Monday by Israel to suspend a permit held by a U.S. Jewish land baron to build 70 homes in Arab East Jerusalem's Ras al-Amoud until an appeal by two Jerusalem city council members against the plan is heard on August 5.
No talks have been held between Syria and Israel since Benjamin Netanyahu became prime minister in June last year.
Syria wants Israel to accept full withdrawal from the Golan Heights, captured by Israel in 1967, before resuming peace talks.
After talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy in Amman, Jordanian Foreign Minister Fayez al-Tarawnah said the suspension of the Jerusalem housing project would advance stalled peace talks.

"We consider this as a confidence-building measure that would hopefully reinstate the trust between the two sides and that would definitely put the Palestinian-Israeli talks on the right course," Tarawnah said.
Israeli-PLO peace talks have been in crisis since March when Israel broke ground on the 6,500-home Har Homa settlement on an East Jerusalem hill known to Palestinians as Jabal Abu Ghneim.
Palestinians demand a halt to settlement activity as a condition to restart peace talks.
Officials in Amman said Mubarak would brief Jordan's King Hussein on Tuesday during a stop at Amman airport on his way back to Cairo after his talks in Damascus.
Tarawnah said Jordan was assured by Levy that Netanyahu was against the Ras al-Amoud settler plan, but sounded a warning that if it did go ahead it would create a setback in peace talks.

Israel, which annexed East Jerusalem after capturing it in 1967, says it can build where it likes in the city it calls its united capital. Palestinians say East Jerusalem will be the capital of their future state.

Tarawnah also cited as a cause for optimism the outcome of talks between Levy and PLO negotiator Nabil Shaath on Monday in which both agreed to renew talks on outstanding issues from a 1995 peace deal.
But PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat was less impressed.
"This was agreed upon one and a half months ago and up until now nothing has happened," he told reporters in Hebron.

Arafat also faced problems closer to home after a panel of Palestinian lawmakers investigating corruption urged him on Tuesday to sack his entire cabinet and put at least one minister suspected of wrongdoing on trial.

The report to the Palestinian Legislative Council specifically recommended trial for Civilian Affairs Minister Jamil al-Tarifi on suspicion of corruption and called for investigations into Planning Minister Nabil Shaath and Transport Minister Ali Kawasmeh
None of the ministers named was immediately available for comment.
